analysis.file_name: 11-03 Why hasn t there been a major financial crisis in recent years .pdf
analysis.title: Why hasn't there been a major financial crisis in recent years?
key_insights: Deutsche Bank Research Institute argues financial crises have not been abolished since 2008, but post-GFC reforms make it harder for shocks to propagate through the traditional banking system, and policymakers are far more willing to intervene early.

Explanations for fewer post-GFC crises: deleveraging after 2008, Basel III and Dodd-Frank reforms, a lower share of financial assets held by banks, fast policy responses, and a shift of debt from private to sovereign balance sheets.
Share of assets held by banks in the FSB's 21 jurisdictions plus the Eurozone fell from a peak of 46% in 2008 to 38% in 2024. The NBFI share rose from 43% to 51%.

Policy response to Covid: the Fed cut 50bp in an emergency move, then another 100bp, resumed QE and opened credit facilities. The ECB's PEPP reached a total envelope of €1.85tn. The credit tightening unwound within months.

In March 2023 the Treasury, Fed and FDIC protected all SVB deposits and the Fed balance sheet briefly expanded. The 2yr Treasury yield fell 61bps on March 13, its biggest daily decline in over 40 years, and the episode did not become a wave of bank failures.

Comparing Q2 2026 with Q2 2016, debt fell for households, financial corporations and nonfinancial corporations. Only government debt rose. Government debt went from the smallest to the largest of the four categories since 2007.
The shift of debt to sovereign balance sheets cushioned private shocks but limited fiscal space. Government bond yields are at multi-year highs and net interest spending is rising.
Future stress may originate outside banks, so historical analysis centred on banking crises may be a less complete guide.

AI: DB judges an AI correction to be a clearer risk than an AI-led systemic crisis at this point. Operating cash flow still funds much of the buildout, borrowing has risen only modestly so far, and valuations are far below the late-1990s.

Under the GHSS framework, meeting both thresholds (3-year rise in business debt of more than 9pp and 3-year real equity rise of over 26%) implies a 45% probability of a crisis within 3 years. The US meets the equity test as of 2025 but not the credit test.
DB's illustrative scenario puts US business-sector leverage just shy of the economy-wide red zone by 2028 if AI capex accelerates and equity prices keep rising 12.5% a year.
US corporate borrowing has accelerated markedly in 2026. Market borrowing costs for US corporates are well above existing average debt service costs, so repricing is still to come.

Private credit: DB says parallels to subprime should not be overstated. The market is similar in dollar size to subprime in 2006-07, but the economy has doubled in nominal terms, the build-up was slower, and redemptions are restricted.
Private credit growth slowed in 2025-26. DB credit strategists flag weaker BDC inflows, rising payment-in-kind interest and refinancing pressure, though defaults remain limited.

Redemption gates give liquidity protection but do not restore solvency. Opacity of end-holders (insurers, other non-banks) makes losses harder to identify. Liquidity support may not work for credit events.

The report states the major central banks are in a rate hiking cycle again. Hiking cycles have regularly coincided with shocks, and higher rates were a contributing factor in the 2023 regional bank failures.
Sovereign stress could feed into NBFIs. IMF data show hedge fund sovereign bond exposures more than doubled since 2022, adding a sovereign-NBFI feedback loop risk similar to the 2022 UK LDI crisis.

DB concludes that with fiscal space constrained and persistent inflation limiting monetary stimulus, the margin for a policy error is limited, and risk tends to be greatest where it is least appreciated.

sector_views.rationale: DB sees an AI correction as a clearer risk than an AI-led systemic crisis. P/E multiples have already corrected since late 2025, most for software, and tech valuations are far from dot-com levels.

risk_factors: An AI capex downgrade from slower demand, financing constraints or supply bottlenecks could cause negative wealth effects and slower capex, and would become systemic if leverage keeps building while AI returns disappoint.
Private credit: slowing growth, rising payment-in-kind interest, BDC inflow weakness, refinancing pressure and opaque exposures among insurers and other non-banks.
Rate hiking cycle by major central banks exposes vulnerabilities, as the 2023 regional bank episode showed.
Sovereign repricing combined with leveraged non-bank amplification and a more constrained policy response.
Limited fiscal space and persistent inflation reduce the capacity for another coordinated policy rescue.

Figure 16 shows IMF estimates that hedge funds' sovereign exposures have more than doubled since 2022.
vol_and_positioning: Hedge fund sovereign bond exposures have more than doubled since 2022 per the IMF, and leveraged hedge fund positions in sovereign markets are flagged as a concern.

tension_points.bull_case: An AI correction would be an economic headwind but not a systemic crisis. Operating cash flow still funds much of the buildout, borrowing has risen only modestly, and valuations are far below late-1990s levels.
tension_points.bear_case: US corporate borrowing accelerated in 2026 and the GHSS-based scenario puts business leverage just shy of the red zone by 2028. Circular financing and off-balance-sheet structures may mean leverage is understated.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Leverage keeps building while AI returns disappoint, raising the likelihood of credit events and amplifying the investment slowdown.

tension_points.bull_case: Defaults remain limited, the build-up was slower, redemptions are restricted and wealth effects are lower, so amplification risk is much more moderate than in 2008.
tension_points.bear_case: Growth is slowing, with weaker BDC inflows, rising payment-in-kind interest and refinancing pressure, and opacity makes losses hard to locate.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Redemption gates cannot restore solvency, so a rise in credit losses and defaults at borrowers would break the orderly-slowdown view.
